items.t: US carries out limited strikes in southern Iran as Trump says talks with Tehran are progressing
items.s: The US military carried out what it called limited airstrikes in southern Iran on Friday, as Trump described them as minor while Qatar-mediated negotiations continue.
p: American forces conducted strikes in southern Iran late on Friday that the military described as limited. The action heightened anxiety across the Middle East and in Gulf states, where many fear that a full-scale war could start again. Doha and Washington both maintain that talks toward a diplomatic settlement are still underway.

Speaking to the media, Donald Trump characterised the operation as a “minor” action aimed at Iranian air defences on Qeshm Island. He said a small anti-aircraft device had been destroyed within minutes. Trump also claimed that Washington had made real headway with Tehran in negotiations that Qatar is leading as chief mediator.

Iranian state media said two missiles struck the Suza area of Qeshm Island, but gave no details about what was targeted or what was damaged. Local residents shared accounts of explosions on social media.
Earlier that day, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard said it had downed a US military drone over the south of the country. Washington has not confirmed that claim.

This is the first strike since the Democratic Party won a significant victory in the midterm elections, a result that officials and analysts have connected to public opposition to Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. It also came after what the US military termed defensive strikes on Monday, when blasts were reported on Qeshm and Hengam islands in the Strait of Hormuz and near Bandar Abbas on the mainland.

Qatar quickly rejected reports that the negotiations had broken down, saying its mediators stayed in close contact with both Washington and Tehran. Two Middle East government officials told AP that Iran is studying Qatari proposals on its nuclear programme. One of them said Tehran still will not discuss its nuclear activities until Washington meets several core demands, among them lifting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, removing sanctions, releasing frozen assets, paying for war damage and ending hostilities across the region. These claims come from anonymous officials and have not been independently verified.

Trump phoned Qatar’s Emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani, according to Qatar’s state news agency. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth also spoke with his Qatari counterpart, the Qatari government said. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reported making calls to at least 12 foreign ministers over two days. On Saturday, an Iranian army spokesman vowed that Iran would not let the enemy rebuild its bases in the region.

Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of Israel’s military intelligence research department and an Iran specialist, wrote on X that Tehran does not fear a renewed clash with the United States and Israel. He argued that, if attacked, Iran would probably try to widen the conflict quickly by hitting Gulf states it considers weak points. His view is a forecast rather than a confirmed plan.
items.cav: The sources do not report casualties or the extent of damage on Qeshm Island. The Iranian drone claim is unconfirmed by Washington, and the description of the strikes as minor comes from Trump. Details of Iran’s conditions rely on anonymous officials. The Al Jazeera item was available only as a summary.
items.op: Calling a strike “minor” does not answer the questions that matter: what was hit, what damage resulted, and what justified it. Gulf states and voters are owed clear answers, not reassurance. If talks are truly progressing, they should be pursued openly, and each strike should face public scrutiny.

items.t: Democrats win midterms on cost-of-living anger, then face limits on economy and Trump probes
items.s: Democrats are heading into Congress with a larger majority than they have had in decades, and they have promised to tackle prices and investigate corruption in the Trump administration. Commentators say both goals will be harder to deliver than the campaign suggested.
p: A Guardian commentary by Eduardo Porter argues that voters’ worries about the rising cost of living drove the midterm results, even though Donald Trump largely ignored the issue. The outcome is likely to give Democrats the largest House majority in nearly four decades and their biggest Senate edge since 2008, the column says.

Porter writes that the new majority will struggle to lower prices for gas, groceries, mortgages and healthcare. Democrats could try to end the war with Iran and reopen the strait of Hormuz, as Senate majority leader-in-waiting Chuck Schumer has suggested, but Trump may not agree, and Democrats lack the 60 Senate votes needed to overcome a filibuster.

Tariffs are another obstacle. Porter notes that after the supreme court struck down Trump’s “national security” tariffs, the administration reimposed many of them under a different statute. He also argues that a budget deficit running at 6% of gross domestic product leaves little room to reverse cuts to Medicaid and food stamps.

Porter also points to a costly investment boom in data-processing centres as a risk to the economy. He cites Goldman Sachs estimates that large hyperscale firms have raised almost $200bn in bond markets so far this year, and he says the tech-heavy Nasdaq has fallen by more than 10% in the last month.

Separately, DW reports that Democrats have pledged to investigate alleged corruption in the Trump administration once they take their seats in January. Analysts expect many of those inquiries to focus on the Trump family’s links to wealthy Middle Eastern countries.

DW cites Trump’s financial disclosures showing his businesses earned about $2 billion in 2025, and a Brian Katulis analysis claiming Gulf entities paid around $300 million to his businesses that year. Much of the income came from the sale of a stake in World Liberty Financial to a firm backed by a senior UAE official. The deal was done in January 2026, shortly before Trump’s inauguration.

DW also reports questions about a Qatari jet worth around $400 million, the Board of Peace, whose funds were reportedly held in a private bank account, and an investigation by CNN into Jared Kushner’s private equity firm. Democratic House Oversight member Robert Garcia has said the Trump family is “the top of our investigative priorities.”
items.cav: The Guardian piece is an opinion column, and its economic forecasts are the author’s judgement rather than reported fact. Many of DW’s figures are second-hand, drawn from CNBC, the Financial Times, CBS and commentators, and the White House has not been shown to have accepted them. None of the alleged conflicts has been established in a legal proceeding.
items.op: Voters who punished the price rises deserve a government that explains what it can and cannot do. Democrats should publish their investigations and the evidence behind them in full, and avoid selective outrage. Transparency, not slogans, will decide whether this majority earns trust.

items.t: Pedro Alliana sworn in as Paraguay’s president after Santiago Peña’s impeachment
items.s: Pedro Alliana assumed Paraguay’s presidency on Friday after Santiago Peña was impeached amid a banking crisis. Peña is under house arrest and faces questioning over alleged offences.
p: Paraguay has a new head of state. Pedro Alliana, who had spent three years as vice president, moved into the top job on Friday after Santiago Peña was removed through impeachment, according to Euronews. The change comes amid a crisis that is both political and financial, triggered by the failure of Ueno Bank earlier this week. Depositors have reportedly lost access to the savings of roughly half of the adult population.
Alliana, now 52, once played basketball at national level and later rose to lead the Colorado Party. Once in office, he said he intends to address the crisis before his mandate ends in August 2028.

Peña is confined to his home in Asunción and is expected to be questioned on Saturday. Prosecutors have named breach of trust, influence peddling and misappropriation of funds as the alleged offences. These remain allegations, and the reporting does not indicate that any court has ruled on them.

Alliana’s rise owed much to Horacio Cartes, a powerful figure in the ruling party. His electoral record includes a defeat in a 2006 bid for the mayoralty of Pilar, his home town, followed two years later by a win in the governorship of Neembucu. He sat in the Chamber of Deputies between 2013 and 2023, presided over that chamber, and then headed the Colorado Party.

Critics have questioned the number of relatives holding public posts, his eldest daughter among them. The alliance with Cartes later frayed. After Cartes withdrew his support, Alliana said on 26 October that loyalty should not be mistaken for “blind obedience.” According to the report, lawmakers pursued Peña’s impeachment but rejected proceedings against Alliana.
items.cav: The sources do not give details of the impeachment vote or the specifics of the Ueno Bank collapse, and the figures on frozen savings are second-hand. The allegations against Peña are claims by prosecutors and have not been tested in court.
items.op: Paraguay’s citizens deserve a clear account of how the bank failed and who is responsible for it. A new president who once shared power with the man now accused must show that the inquiry will be independent, or the country’s trust in its institutions will erode further.

items.t: Trump names immigration hardliner Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff
items.s: President Donald Trump has named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration policy, as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. The move follows Republican losses in the midterm elections and has drawn sharp criticism from Democrats.
p: Trump announced on Friday, in a post on his Truth Social platform, that Miller would take over as chief of staff on Monday, November 9. Miller, 41, has been serving as deputy chief of staff for policy and also holds the title of homeland security adviser. He is widely credited with driving the administration’s mass deportation programme, which has included raids by masked agents.

The appointment came days after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, a result many commentators read as a rebuke of Trump’s agenda. Trump called Miller “one of my most trusted advisers” and praised Wiles, who is moving to what he called the “Trump Political Operation.”

Wiles, 69, said Friday would be her last day in the job. She had announced in September that she was in remission from breast cancer. Al Jazeera reported that she handed her resignation to Trump on Thursday, and a Republican official confirmed the president accepted it. CBS, citing sources, said she had planned to stay until the end of the year or early next year. Earlier, Trump had said there was “zero chance” she would be replaced.

Miller’s record has been contested. The Guardian noted that he helped write the rightwing Project 2025 manifesto. Several outlets pointed to the deaths in January of two protesters in Minneapolis who were shot by immigration agents, an episode that sparked mass demonstrations and intensified criticism of federal enforcement tactics.

Democrats condemned the decision. Chuck Schumer said Trump “couldn’t have made a worse choice,” and Hakeem Jeffries called Miller a dangerous xenophobe and demanded he be fired. Chris Van Hollen described the move as a sign of Trump’s contempt for voters. Robert Garcia, who is expected to chair the House Oversight Committee, said Democrats would continue to investigate Miller. Some Republicans also objected. Congressman Marlin Stutzman, who had earlier said Miller should be fired, called the promotion a “horrible decision.”

Other Republicans and White House figures welcomed the announcement. White House communications director Steven Cheung described Miller as a “Trump OG.” Senators Mike Lee and Eric Schmitt defended his record. The White House said Miller was a key player in delivering the president’s agenda. Miller thanked Trump and said he was honored to serve, writing that the mission was to support the president and defend the Republic.
items.cav: Accounts differ on how Wiles’ departure came about. Al Jazeera and CBS rely on unnamed sources, and the BBC reports that it was unclear whether her deputies would stay at the White House. The sources do not establish whether she was pushed out or chose to leave.
items.op: The chief of staff sits at the centre of White House decision-making, so the public has a stake in how this appointment is handled. Miller’s role in mass deportations and the Minneapolis shootings is disputed and deserves scrutiny, not reward. Trump is signalling that the midterm verdict will not change course. The real test is whether the White House opens its decisions to Congress and the public.

items.t: Palestinian Citizens of Israel Say Post-Election Scrutiny Amounts to a ‘Loyalty Test’
items.s: After Arab parties won a record 19 Knesset seats in October, Palestinian citizens of Israel describe rising suspicion, investigations and pressure. Their account, as reported by Al Jazeera, rests largely on interviews with activists and analysts.
p: Arab parties took a record 19 seats in the Knesset in the October 27 election, a result that analyst Thabet Abu Rass expected the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot would be unable to disregard. According to Al Jazeera, their seats would lift that bloc past the 61-seat mark needed to form a governing coalition.

Lama Yassin, 31, who drove voters to polling stations in her hometown of Arrabeh, told Al Jazeera that the turnout gave her real optimism about change. The debate that followed, she said, was far less welcoming. Israeli broadcasters, in her account, hosted Jewish commentators to discuss Arab voters while barely inviting any Arab participants, and the framing centred on the supposed danger those voters posed.

Within a day of the vote, Likud and figures such as Itamar Ben-Gvir accused the Arab parties of winning through “bribery, threats, violence, forgeries”. The report says these claims kept circulating even after the Central Elections Committee and the Israeli police reported no evidence of organised manipulation.

Yassin argues that Israelis praise Palestinian citizens as partners when it is convenient, yet treat their political ambitions as hostile once they seek real influence over policy. Omar Siksik, a former Tel Aviv-Jaffa councillor, said election day was the only area in which Palestinian citizens stand on equal terms with Jews, and that the Arab vote had come to be seen as a security problem.

The article also describes economic and social pressures. Following October 7, Israel withdrew tens of thousands of work permits held by Palestinians from Gaza and the West Bank, and short-term foreign labourers are reportedly filling those roles. Yassin also pointed to online rumours, circulating over the summer, that Arab doctors were poisoning Jewish patients at Rambam Hospital in Haifa. The report does not say whether those rumours have been checked.

Two legal matters feature prominently. On November 3, around 15 security officers, some masked, raided the Jaffa home of journalist and activist Abed Abou Shehadeh and detained him in front of his two children. He faces an accusation of “contacts with a foreign agent”, and a court ordered him held until November 8. Separately, police detained seven Bedouin men over an alleged plan to pay people to vote for Ra’am, a claim the party disputes. Ayman Odeh, the Arab political leader, is also under investigation by the Shin Bet over allegations that he took foreign money to shape turnout; he rejects them and describes the probe as politically driven.

Abu Rass believes the country has reached a decisive juncture and that Arab citizens now confront the entire state apparatus, and possibly hidden power networks within it. These are his judgements, not findings reported as fact.
items.cav: Most of the serious claims come from interviewees such as Yassin, Siksik and Abu Rass and are presented as their views. The vote-theft allegations, the foreign-funding accusations and the claims about doctors are disputed or unresolved in the report, and it does not report any outcome from the court or Shin Bet proceedings.
items.op: Claims of fraud and foreign funding should be tested in court, not amplified in television studios. When citizens are scrutinised for how they vote and their representatives are treated as a threat, the democratic process itself is at stake. Israeli institutions should prove that the same rules apply to everyone.

items.t: US Secret Service arrests Venezuelan national near White House with three firearms in stolen car
items.s: A man accused of telling officers that voices urged him to kill President Donald Trump was arrested near the White House on Thursday night, according to the Department of Homeland Security. He has been charged and is in US Marshals Service custody.
p: The US Secret Service arrested a man on Thursday evening after officers spotted him acting suspiciously in a parked car on Constitution Avenue in Washington, according to a statement from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The suspect was identified as Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, a Venezuelan national.

According to the DHS account, officers approached the vehicle and the man told them he had heard voices in his head telling him to kill Trump. Officers then found that the car had been reported stolen. The suspect allegedly admitted he had weapons in the vehicle, and officers recovered three firearms, including one rifle, along with dozens of rounds of ammunition.

Chrinos has been charged with multiple offences, including possession of dangerous weapons and theft, the DHS said. He is in the custody of the US Marshals Service. The department also said he had entered the United States illegally through Texas in March 2024, a claim that is presented only in the agency’s statement.

Secret Service Director Sean Curran said the incident reflected a “heightened threat environment” around the White House complex. He said the agency remained confident in its tactics but was alarmed by the rising number of threat cases. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin praised the officers for stopping the man before he could cause harm.

The arrest is the latest in a series of cases in which people have been detained over threats against Trump since he returned to the White House in January 2025, the reports said. The Guardian reported that the secret service and other law enforcement agencies have made similar arrests against people who threatened Trump or his family.

The accounts of the incident come mainly from the DHS statement. The suspect’s description of voices is reported second-hand and has not been tested in court. The White House did not comment on the case and referred questions to DHS and the Secret Service. Chrinos has not yet entered a plea in the reports available, and the charges remain allegations.
items.cav: Nearly all details come from a single DHS statement, including the suspect’s words, the claim of illegal entry and the charges, none of which have been tested in court. The White House declined to comment, and the reports do not say whether the vehicle’s theft has been independently confirmed.
items.op: Threats against a sitting president demand serious policing, but the public is also owed a process in which charges are proven before they define a man. When officials attach immigration status to a case that also involves a mental-health claim, transparency means separating verified facts from political messaging.

items.t: Meghan’s father Thomas Markle charged over child sexual abuse material; no plea entered
items.s: Thomas Markle Sr, father of the Duchess of Sussex, has been charged in the United States with possessing child sexual abuse material, an accusation he has denied. No plea has been entered.
p: US federal agents arrested the 82-year-old in Florida, and the Justice Department says he faces a single charge linked to the alleged images. He was ordered to wear an electronic monitoring device while the case continues, and a court date in California is yet to be set.

At a hearing in Tampa lasting about half an hour, Markle was wheeled in and escorted by two US Marshals, and no plea was recorded. Some outlets describe the arrangement as house detention at his assisted living facility, while others describe a senior care setting in Polk County, so the exact conditions remain unclear.

Investigators say they searched two storage units in the Los Angeles area that Markle had rented since 2008 and seized roughly 78 objects. Prosecutors allege these include negatives, slides and books containing illegal material. A federal complaint says a witness identified Markle in two of the images, which show a man with an underage girl.

Bill Essayli, the first assistant US attorney for central California, said the seized material showed no victims in the country and that the inquiry is ongoing. His office is aware of reports that Markle may have dementia. Markle has rejected the allegations, calling them “sick lies”.

A separate inquiry is under way in the Philippines, where police obtained a warrant to examine devices taken from Markle’s former home in Cebu. His son, Thomas Markle Jr, handed over the material. Philippine officials reported around 7,500 photographs and one video, and an official said some children looked as young as 10 or 11. Forensic checks have not yet established who owned, produced or shared the material.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, said she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations and expressed concern for any children who may have been harmed. She has also said that a letter containing troubling claims about her father reached London’s Metropolitan Police. The force later referred its own handling of that letter to the Independent Office for Police Conduct. Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018.
items.cav: The sources differ on where Markle was held and whether he is under house detention or electronic monitoring. They also disagree on the year the letter reached police, reported as 2019 by the BBC and 2018 by others. Euronews is the only source reporting a probe in Mexico and the Philippine figures, which remain unverified in court.
items.op: Markle is presumed innocent and has not entered a plea, and that presumption must hold in a case this grave. Victims are best served by open court records and clear timelines, not by leaks. The Metropolitan Police’s letter reached one office and went no further, so its referral to the watchdog should be followed through publicly.

items.t: US Launches Another Limited Strike on Iran, Trump Calls It ‘Minor’
items.s: Donald Trump says American forces hit an Iranian air defence system in a fresh, limited strike on Friday. The action came days after an earlier attack became public, while mediators pushed to end the conflict.
p: Trump told reporters on Friday that US forces had destroyed an anti-aircraft installation in Iran. He said Iran had put it together and that it was taken out within roughly five to fifteen minutes, and he called the operation “minor.”

Iranian state media reported hearing two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, located in the Strait of Hormuz. That shipping route is vital for oil and has been thrown into disarray since the US began its war with Iran in February.
The US military had earlier labelled its Monday strikes “defensive.” Blasts were reported that day on Qeshm and Hengam islands, as well as in the nearby mainland area around Bandar Abbas.

The Friday strikes followed a heavy defeat for Trump’s Republican Party in Tuesday’s US midterm elections. Analysts and voters have linked the result to frustration over the handling of the Iran conflict and to higher fuel costs, which the war has pushed up across much of the world economy.

Since the vote, Trump has swung between vowing to “destroy” Iran and saying a settlement is close. The nuclear programme remains the most difficult dispute, and he has insisted it be resolved as part of any agreement to end the fighting.

US Central Command later said on X that Washington would pay up to $20 million, and could offer relocation, to anyone providing information on Iran’s nuclear programme. The notice pointed readers to the State Department’s Rewards for Justice initiative.

Diplomacy is still under way. Trump said on Friday that mediators were continuing their talks with Tehran. Qatar, which has been brokering between Washington and Iran, said US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had spoken with his Qatari counterpart. Trump also spoke with Qatar’s emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani, about lowering tensions, according to Qatar’s ruler’s media office. Concern persists that Trump could still order further strikes.
items.cav: The damage to the air defence system rests on Trump’s own account, and the evidence offers no independent confirmation. The explosions are reported by Iranian state media and are not verified, and no Iranian government response is included.
items.op: When a president calls strikes on another country “minor” in an off-the-cuff exchange, the public must take his word on their scale and purpose. Limited or not, military action needs a clear, checkable account of what was hit and why. A war that is pushing up fuel prices worldwide should not be judged on verbal summaries alone.

items.t: Pope Leo arrives in Uruguay, opening a 12-day South American tour weeks after cancer surgery
items.s: Pope Leo XIV has arrived in Uruguay to begin a 12-day tour of three South American countries, just weeks after lung cancer surgery. The Vatican estimated that 30,000 people turned out to see him in Montevideo.
p: Pope Leo XIV landed in Uruguay on Friday, the first stop on a demanding 12-day tour that will also take him to Argentina and Peru. The 71-year-old pontiff underwent lung cancer surgery only weeks before the trip.

Speaking to reporters aboard the papal plane after a flight of nearly 14 hours from Rome to Montevideo, Leo said he was very happy to be in Uruguay. He said he had never doubted that the journey had to go ahead.

Crowds gathered along his route as he travelled through Montevideo in an open-sided popemobile. The Vatican estimated that 30,000 people came to watch him pass and to attend his first event in the country, which is largely secular and where membership of the Church is declining.

In a speech in the city’s main square, Leo praised respect for the law, negotiation and patient efforts to reach agreements, saying Uruguay could offer these lessons to its neighbours. Uruguayan President Yamandu Orsi, leader of the centre-left alliance, attended the event.

Leo is also expected to visit the Casavalle neighbourhood, an area known for high levels of poverty and violence. According to the reports, his visit is the first by a pope to Uruguay in nearly four decades, since John Paul II came in 1988. Tickets for a prayer vigil at Centenario Stadium sold out within two days.

After three days in Uruguay, the pope will cross into Argentina on Sunday, the homeland of his predecessor Francis, who never returned there as pope. Leo is due to meet President Javier Milei, whose spending cuts the Catholic Church has criticised for hurting programmes for the poor. He also plans to meet business leaders, trade unions and social groups.

The tour ends in Peru on Wednesday, where Leo spent about two decades as a priest and was made a naturalised citizen in 2015. He plans Masses in Chiclayo, Santa Cruz de Succhabamba and Cusco, and a visit to Pucallpa in the Peruvian Amazon to honour indigenous people. Street vendors are selling T-shirts and rosaries bearing his image, and bakeries are selling ‘Leo bread’.
items.cav: The 30,000 crowd figure is a Vatican estimate, not an independent count. The summary describes a 12-day trip, while the article gives only the stops it lists, so the full schedule is not confirmed by the evidence.
items.op: A papal visit can be a moment of faith, but Leo’s message about law, negotiation and patient compromise matters beyond the Church. Governments in the region should be held to that standard, especially where budget cuts fall on the poor.

items.t: Protesters enter Microsoft datacentre construction site in Amsterdam as Europe-wide demonstrations begin
items.s: Demonstrators forced their way onto a building site in Amsterdam where Microsoft is constructing a datacentre, the first action in two days of protests across Europe. Police say they could not stop the occupation and that force was used.
p: On Friday, members of the Dutch direct-action group Geef Tegengas broke into a Westpoort site in Amsterdam where a Microsoft facility is under construction, according to The Guardian and DW. Some climbed a crane, set off flares and attached helium balloons to equipment, while others unfurled banners criticising Microsoft’s dealings with the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Police told NOS, the Dutch public broadcaster, that they had tried to head off the occupation and make arrests but failed, and that force had been used. Protesters said officers deployed teargas against people trying to get in. Crowd estimates differ: DW describes more than 100 activists, while The Guardian, citing organisers and local media, reports hundreds on each side of the fence.

The Amsterdam incident was separate from the wider Stop Dirty Data Centres campaign, a coalition that includes national branches of Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth. Its affiliated members stayed outside the perimeter. The coalition said it had neither organised nor promoted the Dutch action, but described it as understandable that local communities would turn to varied tactics when they feel shut out of decisions.

The campaign says more than 100 groups are taking part in protests in 16 countries and wants a halt to large new datacentre construction until governments set tighter rules. It is not seeking the closure of existing sites. Smaller rallies were held in Bristol, at a datacentre in Berlin, outside Poland’s parliament in Warsaw and in Zagreb, with further demonstrations planned for Saturday in countries including Ireland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, Italy, France and the UK.

Campaigners argue that these sites strain power grids and water supplies, compete with housing for resources and undermine climate targets. Owen Espley, the campaign coordinator, said developments are being pushed ahead with little openness or oversight. Organisers also link the protests to job losses and the influence of technology firms. Roos Molenaar of Geef Tegengas said the Amsterdam project was draining local drinking water, a claim the reports do not independently verify.

Microsoft said it was aware of the demonstration, put the wellbeing of people on and around the site first, and respected peaceful expression while not condoning unlawful acts. Pure Data Centres, the site owner, said it respected peaceful protest but considered entering an active construction site unlawful and dangerous, and asked people to leave and talk through their concerns. DW reports the company plans to invest more than $1 billion (€890 million) in the project.

The protests come amid rising scrutiny of the sector. According to DW, a Google project in Finland faces a criminal investigation over land clearances, and Italy and Portugal are tightening environmental rules for datacentres. The Guardian, referring to a recent investigation with Investigate Europe, reports dangerous conditions for some workers building such sites. DW says the Netherlands has about 200 datacentres planned, under construction or operating.
items.cav: The sources disagree on crowd size, and the claims about the force used come from police on one side and protesters on the other. The drinking-water claim and the campaign’s figures come from the organisers. The Al Jazeera item was only a short summary with no article text, so it adds nothing beyond the basic facts.
items.op: Protest against datacentre expansion is legitimate, but forcing entry onto an active building site is not, and it hands the developers a easy story. Governments that approve these projects owe the public the environmental and labour records behind them, published in full. Openness, not fences, is what would settle this dispute.

items.t: Bomb threats strike European airlines and newsrooms in a third wave this week
items.s: Airlines and media organisations across Europe received bomb threats on Friday. Irish officials said the warnings could be part of a coordinated campaign, though no connection between the two sets of threats has been shown.
p: Friday brought another round of bomb threats against European aviation, the third such episode this week, according to the BBC. Flights travelling to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague and Sofia were among those affected, and authorities said three aircraft were accompanied by Hungarian fighter jets.

The latest round follows a earlier set of warnings that touched close to 30 planes and several European airports. The UK government characterised those threats as a deliberate prank. A Ryanair service due to depart from Lisbon for Rome was one of the flights named, the airline said. AFP counted at least 11 flights targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, while France reported that at least four of its flights had been threatened. Every French flight concerned came down safely.

Media organisations were also forced to act on Friday. Several outlets were evacuated after similar warnings, including Ireland’s public broadcaster RTÉ. Employees at the Irish Independent and at the Dublin premises of NewstalkFM and TodayFM were told to leave their buildings. Sky, the UK broadcaster, said it had also been targeted, a few hours after RTÉ cleared its premises. Sky said it had passed the matter on to the appropriate bodies.

Irish police, the gardaí, confirmed that they were looking into a threat aimed at media organisations in Ireland and elsewhere on the continent. The Irish government said the pattern looked like a probable organised effort to disrupt daily life, yet it admitted it did not know who was behind the messages or whether a single person or a group was responsible. Prime Minister Micheál Martin said he found the situation troubling and that protecting the public came first. Dublin is set to host two major European Union gatherings next week.

The BBC noted that investigators have not tied the airline threats to those sent to newsrooms. Separately, the Russian extremist network “Male State”, which had been named in earlier hoax threats against Italian airports, rejected any role in the warnings. A Telegram channel associated with the network and its founder, Vladislav Pozdnyakov, ridiculed the idea that it had sent the emails, the BBC Russian Service reported.

Al Jazeera reported that newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria also got threats from a caller who gave the name “Mikhail Andropov”. The available material does not verify that name, nor show whether the caller has any link to the other threats.
items.cav: Investigators have not connected the airline and media threats, and the origin of the warnings remains unknown. The denial attributed to “Male State” came through a Telegram account, so it is a claim rather than a verified statement. The “Mikhail Andropov” identity is reported second-hand and has not been confirmed.
items.op: Hoax threats that empty planes and newsrooms impose real costs on ordinary people, so authorities should say plainly what they know and what they are investigating. Vague talk of an organised campaign, without public evidence, leaves citizens to guess. Openness is the best defence against both panic and impunity.

items.t: Schumer vows Democrats will block a ‘rightwinger’ from the Supreme Court as they prepare for Congress
items.s: Chuck Schumer says Democrats will stop Donald Trump from installing a conservative justice on the US Supreme Court. His remarks preview how the party plans to use its expected power when the new Congress convenes.
p: Chuck Schumer, who is set to become Senate majority leader, has said Democrats will stop Donald Trump from installing a conservative justice on the Supreme Court. In an interview with the Associated Press, he said his party would reject what he called “crappy nominees” for the high court, the lower federal courts and the cabinet.

The statement offers a glimpse of the agenda Democrats hope to pursue once the new Congress takes office in January, following midterm victories that returned both chambers to their control. Party leaders are preparing a push back against the president and his policies, according to the Guardian.

Some Democrats are considering investigations into Trump and officials in his administration. Robert Garcia, expected to lead the House oversight committee, told Republicans on Tuesday evening to get legal representation.

Other lawmakers want to advance bills they promised voters. Democrats expect large majorities in both chambers to pass priorities such as reversing Medicaid reductions from Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and ending funding for the war in Iran. Trump has signalled he would veto legislation he opposes.

According to the Guardian, Democrats have won 54 Senate seats for the next Congress, a figure that could reach 56 if their candidates in Mississippi and Alaska prevail. Both contests remain uncalled, though Democrats are ahead in each. As of Friday morning, the party also held at least 253 House seats after gaining more than 40.

Schumer told the AP he expects his party to have the votes needed to reject Trump’s nominees and block other policies. The court currently has a 6-3 conservative majority, built during Trump’s first term with the appointments of Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. Four justices are in their 70s, and the two most conservative, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, are 78 and 76.

Thomas has not signalled any plan to step down. Alito has rejected reports that he will retire, telling Fox News he will remain on the court for the rest of the term regardless of the Democratic result. Any Trump nominee would need confirmation from the Republican-led Senate, which has roughly six weeks left in its session.

Republicans are meanwhile examining their defeat. JD Vance conceded that the Iran war fuelled widespread frustration, Senator Ted Cruz blamed tariffs for higher costs, and Florida governor Ron DeSantis said the party’s vote on the Epstein files looked bad.

Trump’s attention has turned to construction projects in Washington DC. A federal judge halted work on his planned triumphal arch for 14 days, a day after a commission stacked with loyalists approved it. Officials had earlier blamed “vandals” for problems at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, but a Trump-appointed US attorney later found the faults stemmed from poor workmanship. The Guardian also reports that Trump spoke at length about the White House ballroom after the midterms and signed a proclamation barring future presidents from changing the design of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room.
items.cav: This account rests on a single outlet and on Schumer’s own statements about what Democrats will do, which are predictions rather than confirmed actions. Several Senate and House races were still uncalled at the time of reporting, so the seat totals may change. The claims about Thomas and Alito’s retirement plans are second-hand reports.
items.op: Confirmation fights over the Supreme Court are about whether the courts remain a check on power, not only about which party holds a Senate majority. Democrats are right to press for transparency and to scrutinise nominees on their record. The real test will be whether they apply the same standard to every nominee, whichever party is in the White House.

items.t: Fresh bomb threats disrupt at least 18 flights across Europe as media in Ireland and UK are also hit
items.s: A new round of bomb threats on Friday forced disruption to at least 18 flights in Europe and hit media outlets in Ireland and the UK. The aircraft involved landed without incident, and searches turned up no explosives.
p: Flights to or from nine countries, including Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania and the UK, were among those hit by the latest alerts. In Denmark, police looked into a threat aimed at Copenhagen airport, yet the airport’s management stated that operations continued as normal.

Earlier threats on Tuesday and Thursday had already led to at least 35 flights being diverted or searched, which has prompted questions about whether the incidents are coordinated. Eurocontrol, the European air traffic control agency, put Friday’s affected flights at just 0.0674% of the 26,709 flights scheduled across the continent that day. Hungary’s defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, wrote on Facebook that his country had sent fighter jets up three times to accompany civilian planes.

Separately, threats against Irish media organisations interrupted broadcasts, forced staff out of buildings and led police to search offices and newsrooms. National broadcaster RTÉ later returned to its regular schedule. Britain’s Sky News said it had also received a security threat and had informed the authorities. Earlier in the week, cyber-attacks reportedly hit supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, argued that these threats must be treated seriously, describing them as an attempt to spread fear. Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni said she could not confirm whether the hoaxes and cyber-attacks were linked, but she argued that both pointed to civilian infrastructure being targeted. A senior Nato military official said the alliance was following developments and working with its members.

According to several European outlets, a group claiming responsibility sent an email to multiple newsrooms warning of more attacks on transport across the continent. The Guardian said it had decided against publishing the email because its claims could not be verified. Some of Thursday’s threats were signed with a reference to a Russian far-right, ultranationalist movement, but its founder, Vladislav Pozdniakov, denied any involvement in a Telegram post and said the group had been inactive since 2021.

Investigators say they have found no evidence so far that a hostile state or terror group, such as Russia or Iran, is behind the hoaxes, though inquiries remain open. Some officials believe the disruption may be connected to European backing for Ukraine. Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, said investigators needed more time to find those responsible, but added that the recurring pattern looked deliberate. Metropolitan Police chief Mark Rowley urged calm, pointing to the “10p terrorism” era of hoax calls and warning against responding too hastily to every online message.
items.cav: The group’s claim of responsibility and the signatures on the threats are unverified, and the Guardian did not publish the email. Investigators have not named any culprits, and links to Russia or to Ukraine policy are suspicions rather than established findings. The movement’s denial comes from its founder’s own post.
items.op: Threats that stop travellers and frighten staff deserve firm policing, but also public candour about what investigators know. Governments should not let unproven claims harden into policy by default. Europe’s response must be measured, evidence-led and open to scrutiny.

items.t: Midterm results put a crowded field and an open question at the heart of the 2028 race
items.s: Vote counting is still under way in the US midterms, yet both parties are already sizing up their potential 2028 presidential contenders. No one has formally entered the race.
p: Votes were still being tallied when the reports were filed, but the focus has already shifted to who will try to succeed President Donald Trump. According to the BBC, Democrats made large gains in Congress and are expected to head into the 2028 contest with momentum.

Winning the midterms is no guarantee of winning the presidency two years later. The BBC points to Barack Obama, who won a second term in 2012 after Republicans had made huge gains in 2010. For the moment, prospective candidates are working quietly in the background.

Several prominent Democrats who were on the ballot appear to have strengthened their national standing. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff won comfortably in a state that Trump had carried in 2024, and the BBC says his campaign generated several viral moments that raised his profile. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro easily defeated his Republican opponent, and analysts argued that his appeal in a swing state suggests he could be competitive nationally. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also prevailed, in a contest that local commentators had framed as a warm-up for a presidential bid.
California Governor Gavin Newsom was barred from seeking re-election this year, but he still has a stake in a ballot measure that would tax the state’s wealthiest residents, a proposal he opposed.

On the Republican side, Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders both held their seats in Arkansas, though each took only slightly more than half the vote, a narrower showing than before. Exit polls indicate that part of the shift against the party reflected voter anger at the Trump administration. That could make life harder for likely successors who sit in the current leadership, among them Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Vance has tried to put distance between himself and the defeat, as well as a military adventure in Iran that the BBC describes as a political failure for his party. The academic Karen Beckwith, of Case Western Reserve University in Ohio, was quoted by the BBC saying that Vance has been the figure most damaged by the campaign. Rubio has rejected reports that he is weighing a departure from his job before a 2028 bid.

Republicans who sit outside the administration may find it easier to set out their own positions. Senator Ted Cruz, who was not up for election this year, argued that too many party politicians appear indifferent to the economic concerns of voters. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis took a similarly critical line while citing Republican successes in his state.

A French broadcaster’s summary says Democrats face what could become one of the most crowded and unpredictable presidential primaries in decades, with the party still split over whether to move toward the centre or further left. Jim Messina, a former adviser to Obama, told the BBC that dozens of people are already making moves.
items.cav: Vote counting was still ongoing when these reports were published, so the final picture may change. The French source was available only as a short summary, and the description of the Iran operation as a political failure is the BBC’s characterisation rather than an established judgement.
items.op: Midterm winners and losers do not settle who will win in 2028, and voters deserve candidates who explain their plans in public. The party that answers the anger in these results honestly, rather than with slogans, will earn the trust that counts.

items.t: Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie handed 200-year prison term over Shakahola deaths
items.s: According to The Guardian, Paul Mackenzie, leader of a Kenyan doomsday movement, has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the deaths of 190 children and one adult. The term follows a conviction handed down in Mombasa about two weeks earlier.
p: Half of the combined term relates to deaths caused by starvation and half to deaths caused by direct violence, the outlet reported. The sentence concludes a case that has been described as one of the worst cult disasters in recent history.

The verdict was delivered in the coastal city of Mombasa, where the court had found Mackenzie guilty roughly a fortnight before sentencing. Prosecutors argued that, through his church, he pressed followers to deprive themselves and their own offspring of food in the belief that this would spare them at the world’s end. Accomplices reportedly used threats and beatings to enforce those instructions.
Investigators recovered bodies showing severe malnutrition. Some were concealed in crude burial pits and others were dumped in toilet pits. Some victims were reportedly buried while still alive.

The affair came to light in 2023, when a tip led police to arrest Mackenzie. Within weeks, excavations had begun in the Shakahola woodland near the coast in south-eastern Kenya. More than 400 bodies have been retrieved, yet most were so badly decayed that only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie rejected the murder allegations and told the court he had never compelled anyone to fast. The court did not accept that defence. Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache, presiding over a hearing that ran for more than eight hours, said some children had been cut off from food while their parents looked on.

Serious questions remain about how he kept operating. Police searched his premises in 2017, and authorities closed his church in 2019, after which police said he moved to Shakahola. He reportedly barred followers from schooling and from hospital care, calling both satanic. The case has intensified demands for stricter supervision of churches and other faith groups in a country where religion plays a prominent public role.

The judgment addressed 191 deaths, while inquiries into more than 200 further deaths are still open. Mackenzie also faces terrorism and other charges linked to the forest, which he denies. Prosecutors further allege that, while in custody, he directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. He has pleaded not guilty in that case.
items.cav: The conviction and sentence are reported here through a single outlet; the sentencing date and whether the terms run concurrently are not stated. The 52 Kwa Binzaro deaths are prosecutors’ allegations, and the 200-plus other deaths under investigation remain unresolved.
items.op: A sentence of this length is the state’s judgment on the killings, but it is not the whole answer. Kenya’s courts have spoken; the public still deserves a clear account of how a man already on police radar in 2017 kept a congregation under his control for years. Accountability must reach the authorities as well as the accused.

items.t: Kenyan court sentences doomsday cult leader Paul Mackenzie to 200 years for 191 murders
items.s: A Kenyan court has jailed Paul Mackenzie, who led a doomsday cult, for 200 years over the deaths of 191 people, all but one of them children. Twenty-eight others were convicted alongside him.
p: Judge Diana Mochache handed down 100 years for homicide and a further 100 years for starvation-related offences, according to the BBC. Terms within each category run at the same time, while the two categories run one after the other, producing a combined sentence of 200 years.

Prosecutors said Mackenzie directed followers to fast until death in the belief that this would bring their children to heaven. The judge placed the main responsibility for the deaths on him, describing the episode as one of the deadliest cases of cult activity anywhere in the world.

Mackenzie, who presented himself as a pastor, was arrested in 2023, after more than 400 bodies were uncovered in shallow graves in Shakahola forest, close to the coast. The inquiry that followed transfixed the country and attracted attention abroad. He also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he rejects.

The state had asked for the death penalty. Mochache accepted that the case qualified for it to be considered, but she chose not to impose it, reasoning that execution would close off any chance of reform. The BBC notes that Kenya has not executed anyone since 1987.

The judge described the killings as deliberate and planned, and said the accused showed no regret, some even announcing they were prepared to starve themselves. A co-accused reportedly told followers that anyone who refused to fast should be pushed toward heaven by force, the BBC reports. Graves inside the forest were given the name of weddings.

Post-mortem examinations found that starvation accounted for most deaths, while others involved suffocation, strangulation or injuries to the head. For some victims the cause could not be established because the bodies had decomposed, and several people died shortly after being rescued because they were badly undernourished.

The case has also raised questions about oversight. Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights concluded that local administrators and police had repeatedly failed to act on the cult’s activities. Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives, said he went to the police in March 2023 and expected an immediate rescue that never came. A commission of inquiry set up by President William Ruto was later ruled invalid on constitutional grounds.
items.cav: The sources give 191 murders but more than 400 bodies were found; the evidence does not explain how the court arrived at its count or how the two figures relate. Wanje’s account of police inaction is his own and is not independently confirmed in the evidence. The evidence does not say whether the sentence can be appealed or whether the separate charges have a timetable.
items.op: A long sentence does not answer the question of how a cult operated for so long under official eyes. Kenya owes the Shakahola families a full public account of which officials knew what was happening, and why they did nothing. Justice has been done in court, but accountability for the state’s inaction remains unfinished.

items.t: Hoax bomb threats force searches and diversions across European flights
items.s: A wave of bomb threats against commercial flights led to searches, diversions and emergency alerts across Europe this week. Authorities said no explosives were found where checks were reported.
p: Hoax bomb threats targeted commercial flights across Europe this week, according to live reporting by The Guardian, which said at least 35 planes had been searched or diverted before Friday. Multiple flights were diverted or forced to make emergency landings, prompting security checks and wider disruption.

A Romanian airline, Tarom, flight from Prague to Bucharest was among the latest believed to be affected. The aircraft sent a squawk code of 7700, the general emergency signal, before landing safely in Bucharest. The Dutch military police confirmed that it had checked a KLM flight to Amsterdam after a bomb threat and that no explosives were on board. The statement did not name the flight. Local Dutch media said it had come from Prague, and the Guardian identified it as KL1350 on that basis.

Hungary’s defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, said on Facebook that fighter jets had been scrambled three times to escort civilian flights in Hungarian airspace after reported threats. The alerts included a WizzAir flight from Brussels to Sofia and flights from Prague to Cyprus and Bucharest.

The Prague airport told the Guardian that nine flights had been affected by bomb threats so far that day. A spokesperson said police had taken the necessary security measures and that “Operations at Prague Airport remain unaffected.” Later, the spokesperson told AFP that at least eight flights to and from Prague had been hit, naming incoming routes from Denmark, Spain and the UK and outgoing routes to the Netherlands, Cyprus, Romania, Italy and the UK.

Copenhagen police said they had completed checks at the Danish capital’s airport and had been present only as a security measure. They said they did not assess there to be any danger to passengers or others using the airport, and that they were investigating the new threats. A Bulgarian transport ministry spokesperson told AFP that alerts had also been received for two flights to Sofia, and that both had landed safely.

Flight-tracking data from FlightRadar24 showed planes circling near Prague, with at least four holding near the airport. An AJet service from Istanbul diverted to Vienna after several circles over Prague, but the Guardian said there was no suggestion that it was affected by the threats. The Guardian also reported that at least 17 flights had been disrupted, although details from airports and national authorities had become harder to collect. Eurocontrol’s daily counter put the number of flights in Europe that day at 26,709.
items.cav: The sources do not agree on exact numbers: the Prague airport gave nine and then eight affected flights, and the reported total of disrupted flights is “at least” 17 without a full list. The identification of the KLM flight comes from local media, not from the Dutch police. The AJet diversion is not linked to the threats by any source.
items.op: Hoaxes that empty skies and tie up fighter jets carry real costs, and the public deserves to know how they are being handled. Airports and police should publish consistent, timely counts and clear confirmations of what was found. Reassurance without transparency only leaves passengers guessing.

items.t: Iran Widens Diplomacy to Moscow and Gulf as Washington Weighs Renewed Strikes
items.s: Iran is pressing diplomatic channels with Russia and Gulf states while the United States signals it could resume large-scale military action. Tehran has set seven conditions before it will discuss its nuclear programme or reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
p: Tehran's outreach comes as Donald Trump has hinted that Washington could return to full-scale strikes on the Islamic republic. Citing a US official, the news website Axios reported that US Central Command was readying for major operations and was only awaiting instructions from Washington. On Thursday, Trump said the US might need to wipe out what remains of Iran's capabilities, and suggested the world would find out soon whether he acts.

Friction escalated after Iranian forces brought down two American reconnaissance drones near Qeshm island in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after the US had hit targets earlier in the week. Iranian officials have signalled a response should larger American strikes follow.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran had passed Washington a fresh nuclear and peace proposal through Qatari intermediaries, but would only weigh it once the US accepts its seven demands. Those demands reportedly include sanctions relief, the release of frozen Iranian funds and an end to the American naval blockade around Iranian ports near the Strait. Reuters said Washington is reviewing the offer. The US position, by contrast, is that an agreement on Iran's nuclear capacity must form part of any ceasefire before broader talks can resume.

Mohsen Rezaei, Iran's top security official, travelled to Moscow and met Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin carrying a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, though Iranian state media gave no details of its substance. Rezaei called the encounter a highly significant exchange, according to the Iranian embassy. He also said the sides had discussed plans for gas pipelines linking Russia and Iran, which he framed as a remedy for Iran's gas shortages and a route for Russian energy exports to neighbouring countries.

The Financial Times has reported that Russia earlier agreed to provide Iran with 90 helicopter-mounted launchers for precision-guided missiles, despite its own demand for weaponry in the war in Ukraine. The paper based this on a Russian defence manufacturer's production schedule for 2024 and 2025, where the order was logged under a code associated with Iran. Tehran has previously supplied Shahed drones, and Russia has reportedly assisted Iran with supersonic cruise missiles and Verba portable anti-air missiles. Nicole Grajewski of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace told the paper the arrangement suggested Moscow was less troubled by Western objections than before.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke on Thursday with counterparts from the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Turkiye, Qatar and Oman about de-escalation and regional stability. Oman's foreign ministry said safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz was a central topic. Separately, Russia's Foreign Ministry urged its citizens not to travel to Iran, pointing to lingering risks of renewed escalation. Senior Iranian officials have warned that any state assisting a US attack on Iran would become a legitimate target.
items.cav: The Financial Times figures on the helicopter-mounted launchers come from documents the paper said it examined, and the evidence does not show an official Russian or Iranian response. Iran's claims about its gas refineries and the contents of Rezaei's message from Khamenei remain unverified, and the Kremlin's readout is not described in the sources.
items.op: Diplomacy is welcome, but seven preconditions and open threats of renewed bombing leave civilians and shipping in the Gulf exposed. Any ceasefire should be built on public terms that all sides can be held to. Secret arms deals and closed-door messages make that harder, and the public has a right to know them.

items.t: Russian-linked group denies role in Europe-wide bomb hoax threats to flights
items.s: A group named in hoax bomb threats to Italian airports has denied any involvement, as flights across Europe received warnings this week. No explosives have been found so far.
p: An Aer Lingus flight bound for Rome was redirected to a French military base after receiving a bomb warning. It was one of many alerts reported across the continent this week, including a Ryanair service from Rome to Lisbon and a Wizz Air rotation from Prague to Rome that ended up in Venice.

The “Male State”, an extremist group with misogynistic views, was named in the threats sent to Italian airports. A Telegram account linked to the group and to its founder, Vladislav Pozdnyakov, told the BBC Russian Service that it had no connection to the emails, saying the group had not existed for many years. The same channel claimed that the group had placed explosives on two inbound aircraft, but no independent source has confirmed this.
Russia banned the group in 2021, and Pozdnyakov is thought to be living abroad. In some places the organisation now calls itself “Male Legion”.

The first hoax message, which the BBC has seen, was sent on Thursday morning to several staff members and departments at Aeroporti di Roma, the firm that runs Rome's airports, as well as to accounts at Fiumicino. The sending address seems to be tied to state health services in Bogota, Colombia. The text, written in fluent Italian, said the group had planted explosives on two incoming planes as an assault on what it called Italy's feminist establishment.

Authorities diverted one of those planes to France, and Italian air force jets escorted the other into Rome. Searches found no explosives on either aircraft or on any other flight that reported a threat. A source at the Rome airport operator said such warnings were highly unusual and could not recall anything comparable in recent years.

On Friday, several prominent Irish media organisations also received bomb threats, leading to evacuations. The Irish government said the incidents appeared to be a coordinated effort to cause disruption. It is not clear whether airports or airlines in other countries received the same or similar threats, and at least one Friday warning appears to have been made by phone rather than email.

La Stampa, an Italian newspaper, has asked whether the group is acting as an armed arm of the Russian state, and it appears convinced of the group's responsibility. Bellingcat, which examined the group in 2022, described it as a loud and hostile online supporter of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Italy's defence minister, Guido Crosetto, said a deliberate effort appears to be underway to deepen chaos. He tied the hoax calls to other recent disruptions, including cyber attacks that pushed up supermarket refrigerator temperatures and problems with France's blood supply. Investigators across Europe are still working out who sent the threats and whether they were coordinated or copied by others.
items.cav: The attribution to the group is disputed: it denies involvement, and the claim of responsibility comes from a channel whose authenticity is not independently confirmed. The Colombian link is only described as an apparent connection, and Crosetto's wider linking of incidents is his own assessment.
items.op: Blaming a group before investigators have established who sent the threats risks confusing the public and rewarding whoever sends them. Authorities should publish what they can verify, and newspapers and ministers should separate evidence from suspicion. Trust in air safety depends on clear, checkable facts.

items.t: Bomb threats hit Irish broadcaster RTE as flight disruption spreads across Europe
items.s: Irish public broadcaster RTE evacuated its buildings after a bomb threat on Friday, adding media to the targets of a wave of threats that has disrupted flights across Europe. Dublin hosts a high-level EU meeting two days later.
p: Media organisations in Ireland were drawn into a campaign that had already grounded aircraft across the continent for several days. On Friday, RTE said its premises had been cleared after a threat was received, and other news outlets were also reviewing their security.

An RTE reporter said the group that claimed responsibility for Friday’s threats was the same one that had targeted airlines earlier in the week. Irish Deputy Prime Minister Simon Harris told Cork 96FM radio that it remained unclear whether a lone individual or a coordinated network was behind the campaign.

Taoiseach Micheál Martin called the situation “worrying”. He said the Gardaí (Irish police) and the Defence Forces were investigating who was responsible. Martin also asked any organisation that gets a similar warning to treat it seriously and inform the police, so investigators can piece together a fuller picture.

According to RTE’s account of his remarks, Martin said the episode showed how little it takes to disrupt daily life and unsettle people through unconventional tactics. When asked whether the threats were linked to the EU meetings planned for Dublin, he stressed the need to keep those gatherings on schedule, pointing to the number of prime ministers attending and the heavy security planning this demands.

More than two dozen flights were affected by threats this week, and further incidents were reported on Friday. Police in Denmark and the Czech Republic also responded to threats that later turned out to be false. A Tarom service travelling from Prague to Bucharest was warned, yet reached its planned destination before officials concluded the threat was baseless.

Police in Copenhagen said officers had attended the airport for a second consecutive day in connection with threats aimed at air traffic. They added that passengers faced no danger and that flights had not been disrupted.

The report stresses that bomb threats are not rare, but a run of them in such a short span is out of the ordinary. It sets the episode against rising geopolitical tension with Russia and a string of hybrid attacks that have unsettled Europe. The sources do not say who is responsible or whether any connection to those tensions has been established.
items.cav: The summary describes newsrooms evacuated across Ireland, but the article reports the evacuation only at RTE, with other organisations taking unspecified security measures. The claim that the same group sent threats to airlines and media comes from an RTE reporter and has not been confirmed by officials. Links to Russia are presented as context, not as established fact.
items.op: Threats designed to frighten should not be allowed to hollow out public life. The answer is transparency: officials should explain the investigation as it proceeds, so newsrooms, airlines and citizens can judge the risk rather than guess. Reporting every threat to police, as the Taoiseach urged, is the right instinct.

items.t: Global stocks tumble as tech fears follow Democrats’ midterm win
items.s: Asian markets fell sharply after a heavy sell-off on Wall Street, as investors worried that a Democratic midterm victory could slow the tech investment boom. The Guardian’s live business coverage tracked the losses.
p: Markets across the Asia-Pacific region opened deep in the red after Wall Street suffered steep losses, according to the Guardian’s rolling business coverage. Investors fear that the Democrats’ strong performance in this week’s midterm elections could curb spending on the tech sector’s growth engine.
Japan’s Nikkei lost almost 6%, its steepest one-day fall since April 7 2025, when tariff worries rattled investors. South Korea’s KOSPI slid 6.7%, while Taiwan’s TAIEX shed 4.5%, the report said.

The Guardian reported that more than $3.2tn was erased from the US stock market the previous day. The Nasdaq tech index fell 5.5%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, and the S&P 500 declined 4.36%.

Makers of memory chips, which had benefited most from the tech spending wave, bore the brunt of the selling. SanDisk dropped 22%, and both Micron and AMD gave up 17% of their value, according to the same account.

Christopher Forbes, head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets, described the session as “a bit of a disaster”. He told Reuters that clients were facing margin calls and complaints, and suggested the shift could signal a wider policy pullback affecting data centres, approvals and equity fundraising.

Analysts blamed policy uncertainty. Democrats have been more critical of data centres, a stance that could slow the build-out of new computing capacity, particularly given public unease about the sector. Kyle Rodda of Capital.com called the selling a “brutal sell-off”.

The Guardian noted that nerves were already present before the vote. Overall earnings have disappointed, with the Magnificent Seven companies falling short of growth forecasts and hinting that spending is cooling. The Nasdaq Composite remains up 4.6% since January, though it is more than 10% below its peak.
Traders are also waiting for the latest US jobs report, which may shed light on the strength of the labour market.
items.cav: All figures and quotes come from a single live-blog summary by The Guardian, and the report links the sell-off to the midterms through analysts’ interpretation rather than direct evidence. The summary does not explain which Democratic policies would be enacted, and the $3.2tn figure is not independently confirmed here.
items.op: Markets are right to question who bears the cost of a tech boom built on lofty valuations. Policy uncertainty should be settled through open rules and public debate, not left to investor panic. Clear, transparent rules for data centres would serve savers far better than sudden swings in sentiment.

items.t: Pope Leo XIV sets off on South America tour, starting in Uruguay
items.s: Pope Leo XIV left Rome on Friday for a tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, which DW describes as the longest and farthest trip of his papacy so far. The Vatican says he is in good health, while DW reports that he is recovering from recent cancer surgery.
p: The pope’s departure from Rome took place shortly after 7 am on Friday, according to the Vatican. Leo is due to touch down in Montevideo, the Uruguayan capital, in the late afternoon local time. The Chicago-born pontiff is starting a journey that will also bring him to Argentina and to Peru, a country where he spent years as a missionary and later as a bishop.

Leo’s schedule in Uruguay runs for three days. He will hold talks with President Yamandú Orsi and speak to government officials and diplomats. He is also set to lead Vespers at the Montevideo Metropolitan Cathedral and to visit a neighborhood marked by gang violence. Trips to Paysandú and Florida are planned later in the visit.

From Uruguay the pope moves on to Argentina, with stops in Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Luján. Euronews names these cities but does not mention political meetings. DW reports that Leo is expected to meet President Javier Milei, whose spending cuts have drawn criticism from the Church for hurting social programmes. DW adds that he also plans to meet business figures, unions and social groups.

In Peru, Euronews lists Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa as stops. DW says the pope will also say Mass in the mountain village of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba and will go to the Amazon city of Pucallpa to meet indigenous communities. DW also points out that Peru’s Catholic population has dropped from 76% in 2013-2014 to roughly 67%.

Leo’s health is a point of uncertainty. DW says the 71-year-old is recovering from lung cancer surgery performed only three weeks ago. Euronews quotes Maria Montserrat Alvar, the Vatican’s new communications chief, who described the pope’s stamina as excellent and said his doctors feel “very confident”.

DW describes Uruguay as the most secular country in Latin America. It was the first nation to legalise recreational marijuana and has since approved abortion, same-sex marriage and assisted dying, all over Church objections. Even so, tickets for his prayer vigil at Montevideo’s Centenario Stadium sold out within two days.

DW also notes that Latin America holds about 40% of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics, though fewer people there now identify as Catholic. In Argentina, DW cites Pew Research Center figures showing that the share of Catholics fell from roughly 71% at the start of Francis’s papacy to 58% by 2024.
items.cav: Euronews and DW both describe the Peru stops, and DW adds one Mass site, so the two lists do not conflict. Euronews does not mention a meeting with Milei, which appears only in DW, and the cancer surgery is reported by DW alone. The Vatican’s reassurance about the pope’s health comes through a Euronews quotation.
items.op: A papal tour is a religious event, but the public has a fair interest in the health of a 71-year-old leader on a long journey. Official reassurances are welcome, yet they cannot replace clear, direct information. The Vatican should be open about the pope’s condition so that the faithful and observers can judge for themselves.

items.t: Court pauses work on Trump’s Washington arch for two weeks
items.s: A federal judge has put a 14-day hold on building the 250-foot arch Donald Trump wants in Washington, DC. The hold came shortly after a federal planning panel signed off on the design.
p: Judge Tanya Chutkan issued the order on Friday, according to Al Jazeera. The administration had said building could start as early as Thursday, so the pause arrives just before work was expected to begin.
The National Capital Planning Commission backed the project by 8-4 after a nine-hour session on Thursday. Dozens of people who oppose the arch spoke against it during that session.

The decision comes amid several lawsuits against the project. A group of Vietnam War veterans filed one in February. Their filing argues that the arch, planned near Arlington National Cemetery, could obstruct the sightline between the graves and the Lincoln Memorial, a view they describe as deliberately designed to represent national unity.
Trump first floated the arch last year as a way to commemorate the country’s 250th anniversary. He has pointed to Paris’s Arc de Triomphe, completed in 1836, as a model.

The arch is one of several Washington projects Trump has put forward. On Friday he also signed a proclamation turning the Oval Office and Cabinet Room into a national monument. Al Jazeera noted that judges have previously blocked many of his plans, and that Democrats’ midterm victories this week could bring those plans under closer review.
items.cav: The sources describe the pause as temporary and do not say what happens when it ends or how the court will rule on the merits. The veterans’ sightline concerns are claims made in their filing and have not been tested in court. NPR’s summary is brief and does not give the court details or the planning vote.
items.op: Monuments meant to unite a nation should be approved through open, accountable review that gives objectors a real hearing. An 8-4 vote after dozens of objections does not by itself show the process was sound. Courts should test it, and the government should welcome that scrutiny.

items.t: Iranians Uncertain After Trump Midterm Setback as Repression Continues
items.s: Iranian officials have celebrated the Republican midterm losses as a rejection of Trump’s war, while people interviewed inside Iran say they expect repression at home to continue whatever happens in Washington, according to The Guardian.
p: Within hours of the US midterm results, which dealt a heavy blow to the Republican party, supporters of the regime gathered in Tehran’s Enghelab Square and burned a large banner depicting Donald Trump, JD Vance, envoy Steve Witkoff and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Officials have since made combative statements framing the losses as a verdict against Trump’s war on Iran, according to The Guardian.

Supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father Ali Khamenei was killed in strikes in February, declared that the American system was already breaking down. The report adds that state television aired a staged hanging of Trump in Tajrish Square, with an actor wearing a Trump mask and an orange jail uniform.

Among ordinary Iranians the atmosphere is far more guarded. Many point to a deteriorating economy and do not know what Trump’s setback will mean for their lives. Mehnaz, a Tehran-based journalist, described a mood close to hopelessness, with people trying to work out what comes next.

Some of the people Mehnaz has spoken to think the midterm loss raises the risk of a renewed full-scale war, since Trump no longer needs to face voters. She is more worried about the regime itself, which she says has been executing people every day, and she expects that to continue with or without a war.
The Oslo-based group Iran Human Rights (IHR) reports that at least 696 people have been executed in Iran this year. The article does not explain how that count was assembled.

Alborz, a 36-year-old writer in Tehran, describes shops where people still browse but rarely buy, because prices have climbed so steeply that a single T-shirt now costs what a suit did a year ago. He also says people around him believe a full-scale war is less likely now, though he adds that no one can be certain.

Noor, 24, from Karaj, spent three weeks in prison after joining protests in January and says she was arrested during the war. She describes the security apparatus as a “well-oiled machine” that keeps working whatever the state of the conflict. Asked about the days ahead, she said no one inside the country can predict what comes next, adding that people have been bracing for the worst all year.

Moein, a medic in central Iran, says he had underestimated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, both the loyalty of its members and its strategic skill. He sees a painful paradox in a state that has survived decades of sanctions yet turns its coercive power on its own citizens.
